subject: Climate & Environment
title: Megadroughts Past and Future
description: A 60-second lesson on Megadroughts Past and Future.

hook.text: Tree rings reveal droughts that lasted decades — far worse than anything in recorded history.

buildup.text: The American Southwest experienced a megadrought from 2000 to 2022 — the driest in 1,200 years.

discovery.text: Lake Mead, which supplies water to 25 million people, dropped to just 27% of capacity.

twist.text: Scientists say climate change made this drought 72% worse than it would have been naturally.

climax.text: As the planet warms, megadroughts will become more frequent and more severe in dry regions.

punchline.text: History hid the worst droughts in tree rings. The future won't be so quiet.

quiz.question: How long did the recent American Southwest megadrought last?

details.summary: Megadroughts lasting 20 years or more have occurred naturally throughout history, and tree-ring records reveal a current megadrought in the American Southwest is the driest in 1,200 years. Climate change is raising the probability of multi-decade droughts across vulnerable regions.
details.whyItMatters: Modern water infrastructure was built during a relatively wet period. Megadroughts expose the fragility of water systems that serve hundreds of millions of people.
takeaways: The current western US drought is the worst in at least 1,200 years
Roughly 40 percent of the drought's severity is attributable to warming
Lake Mead and Lake Powell dropped to record low levels

faq.question: What caused the current megadrought in the American West?
faq.answer: Natural variability reduced precipitation, but climate change amplified the drought by roughly 40 percent through increased evaporation and earlier snowmelt. The combination pushed the drought to levels not seen in over a millennium.

faq.question: How do scientists reconstruct ancient droughts?
faq.answer: Tree rings record annual growth, with narrow rings indicating dry years. Networks of tree-ring records across the West create a continuous moisture history spanning over 2,000 years, revealing past megadroughts that lasted decades.
